author: reek
body: QR encoding for hardware telemetry -- safety recommendation R-1 of the silent-keyboard account. A machine with no serial port and no working disk write can still be READ: it renders its findings as QR codes on the framebuffer, a human photographs the glass with whatever camera is in their pocket, and the decoder turns the photo back into exact bytes. No transcription, no OCR, no dependence on the subsystem under test. The human-readable status lines stay on screen beside the codes, so the person holding the camera also knows whether the news is good.

author: reek
body: Everything through the matrix is pure computation over small buffers, so the battery can verify it without a device; only the final draw touches the framebuffer, through GopDraw.

author: reek
body: The generator polynomial is the product of (x - a^i) for i in 0..25, built by repeated multiplication so no coefficient table is trusted to memory. g[j] is the coefficient of x^j; g[26] ends up 1.

author: reek
body: Synthetic division of the message (as the high-order coefficients) by the generator; what remains in the tail is the 26 ECC codewords. The division CONSUMES the message positions as it eliminates each leading coefficient (the monic generator's top term XORs work[i] with itself), so the data is copied back in afterwards -- the work buffer is then the final codeword sequence: data, then ECC.

author: reek
body: Text in, 37x37 module plane out (byte per module, 1 dark). The caller may keep the buffer as long as it likes; nothing here is retained.

author: reek
body: The ECC tail of the codeword buffer, exposed for the battery test to pin against an independent Reed-Solomon computation.

author: reek
body: One matrix row as a line of 0s and 1s, for serial verification and the battery's frozen expectation.

author: val
body: One fixed shape, no tables: version 5, byte mode, error level L -- a 37x37 module matrix carrying up to 106 bytes in a single Reed-Solomon block of (134, 108). Fixed version means fixed alignment pattern, fixed format layout, no version-info block (that starts at version 7), and a single code path that a battery test can pin. Payloads beyond 106 bytes split across several codes, each chunk prefixed "i/n;" so the decoder can reassemble from one photograph. Mask pattern 0 is applied unconditionally: mask CHOICE is a readability optimization in the spec, not a correctness requirement, and a fixed mask keeps the encoder deterministic.

author: val
body: GF(256) with the QR polynomial 285. One buffer holds both tables: exp at offset 0 (exp of 0..254; index 255 wraps to 1 harmlessly), log at offset 256.

author: val
body: Byte mode: indicator 0100, an 8-bit count (versions 1-9), the bytes, a 4-bit terminator, zero-pad to the byte boundary (already zero in a fresh buffer), then the spec's alternating pad bytes 236 and 17 out to the 108 data codewords. The slice form encodes a prefix (a chunk tag like "2/4;") followed by a character range of a larger text, so a long payload can spread across several codes without a substring ever being built.

author: val
body: Fifteen bits: two bits of error level (L = 01), three of mask id, ten of BCH remainder (generator 1335), the whole thing XORed with the spec constant 21522 so it is never all-zero.

author: val
body: Two parallel 37x37 byte planes: m holds the modules (1 dark), fn marks function modules the data placement must step around. The reserved rectangles overlap the timing lines at two corners; the flag is idempotent so the overlap is harmless.

author: val
body: The standard zigzag: two-module columns from the right edge, up then down, hopping over the timing column between the pairs (8,7) and (5,4). Data bits stream MSB-first out of the 134 codewords; the seven remainder bits past the end are zero. Mask 0 flips a module when row + column is even, applied only to data modules -- which is every module this walk touches.

author: val
body: Both copies, most significant bit first, exactly where the spec puts them. The second copy runs up the left edge of the bottom-left finder and across the bottom of the top-right one.

author: val
body: White quiet zone of four modules on every side -- the spec minimum, and the thing screens are usually worst at giving a camera. Dark modules are true black on true white for the full contrast the sensor can get.
